clinicalPearls: A rare lobular panniculitis that develops after rapid reduction or withdrawal of high-dose systemic corticosteroids, most often described in children.
Firm, tender subcutaneous nodules and plaques appear typically within days to a few weeks of dose reduction.
Lesions favour sites where corticosteroid-induced fat had accumulated, notably the cheeks, and may also affect the trunk and proximal limbs.
The classic history is a child treated with high-dose corticosteroids (for example for rheumatic or neoplastic disease) whose therapy is tapered too quickly.
Histology closely resembles subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn, with needle-shaped crystal clefts within adipocytes and a granulomatous, lipophagic infiltrate.
The eruption is generally self-limiting and resolves over weeks to months without specific treatment.
Reinstituting corticosteroids and then tapering more gradually may hasten resolution in symptomatic cases.
Recognition avoids unnecessary investigation for infection or relapse of the underlying disease.
reference.pathophysiology: During high-dose corticosteroid therapy, lipid composition of subcutaneous fat shifts towards a higher proportion of saturated fatty acids with a raised melting point, and corticosteroids promote redistribution and accumulation of fat at characteristic sites. When corticosteroids are abruptly withdrawn, the altered, saturated-fat-rich adipose tissue is prone to crystallisation and necrosis. Liberated fatty acids provoke a lobular, lipophagic granulomatous inflammatory reaction, and histology reveals radial needle-shaped crystal clefts within adipocytes and giant cells, closely mirroring subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn. Gradual tapering allows the fat composition to normalise and prevents the crystallisation that underlies the panniculitis.
additionalDifferentials: subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn (in infants)
relapse of the underlying inflammatory or neoplastic disease with cutaneous involvement
additionalInvestigations: deep skin biopsy for histopathology (needle-shaped crystal clefts, lobular granulomatous panniculitis)
review of the corticosteroid tapering schedule and timing relative to lesion onset
serum calcium to exclude associated hypercalcaemia
inflammatory markers and cultures to exclude infection
assessment for relapse of the primary disease that prompted corticosteroid use
full blood count and metabolic panel
redFlags: features suggesting infection (fever, fluctuance, systemic upset) rather than sterile panniculitis
hypercalcaemia analogous to that seen in neonatal fat necrosis
signs of relapse of the underlying disease requiring corticosteroid reinstatement
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and self-limiting, resolving spontaneously over weeks to months, particularly when corticosteroids are tapered more gradually.
pitfalls: Mistaking the nodules for infection or for relapse of the treated disease and escalating therapy inappropriately.
Failing to link lesion onset to a recent corticosteroid taper.
Overlooking possible hypercalcaemia given the histological similarity to neonatal fat necrosis.
Sampling too superficially to capture the diagnostic lobular fat changes.
Reintroducing corticosteroids without then planning a slower taper.
